original_txt: \xe2\x80\x9cFileless\xe2\x80\x9d UAC Bypass using sdclt.exe | enigma0x3 Red Teamer and Security Addict enigma0x3 Post navigation \xc2\xab Bypassing UAC using App\xc2 Paths Defeating Device Guard: A look into\xc2 CVE-2017-0007 \xc2\xbb \xe2\x80\x9cFileless\xe2\x80\x9d UAC Bypass using\xc2 sdclt.exe March 17, 2017 by enigma0x3 Recently, I published a post on using App Paths with sdclt.exe to bypass UAC. You may remember that the App Path bypass required a file on disk. Since sdclt.exe is out there, I figured I would publish another bypass using that binary, only this one is fileless. I mentioned it in my previous post, but the Vault7 leak confirms that bypassing UAC is operationally interesting, even to nation states, as several UAC bypasses/notes were detailed in the dump. As far as public bypasses go, definitely check out the UACME project by @hfiref0x, which has a nice collection of public techniques. In newer versions of Windows, Microsoft has shown that they are taking the bypasses seriously. This has motivated me to spend a little more time on UAC and the different methods around it. As some of you may know, there are some Microsoft signed binaries that auto-elevate due to their manifest. You can read more about these binaries and their manifests here. While searching for more of these auto-elevating binaries by using the SysInternals tool \xe2\x80\x9csigcheck\xe2\x80\x9c, I came across \xe2\x80\x9csdclt.exe\xe2\x80\x9d and verified that it auto-elevates due to its manifest: *Note: This only works on Windows 10. The manifest for sdclt.exe in Windows 7 has the requestedExecutionLevel set to \xe2\x80\x9cAsInvoker\xe2\x80\x9d, preventing auto-elevation when started from medium integrity. As I mentioned in my last post, a common technique used to investigate loading behavior on Windows is to use SysInternals Process Monitor to analyze how a process behaves when executed. I often work some basic binary analysis into my investigative process in order to see what other opportunities exist. One of the first things I tend to do when analyzing an auto-elevate binary is to look for any potential command line arguments. I use IDA for this, but you can use your preferred tool. When peering into sdclt.exe, I noticed a few arguments that stood out due to interesting keywords: These were interesting as sdclt.exe is set to auto-elevate in its manifest anyway. Looking at sdclt.exe in IDA, it checks if the argument matches \xe2\x80\x9c/kickoffelev\xe2\x80\x9d. If it does, it sets the full path for \xe2\x80\x9csdclt.exe\xe2\x80\x9d, adds \xe2\x80\x9c/KickOffJob\xe2\x80\x9d as a parameter and then calls SxShellExecuteWithElevate. Following that path, SxShellExecuteWithElevate starts \xe2\x80\x9c%systemroot%\\system32\\sdclt.exe /kickoffjob\xe2\x80\x9d with the \xe2\x80\x9cRunas\xe2\x80\x9d verb. This is essentially programmatically executing the \xe2\x80\x9cRunAsAdministrator\xe2\x80\x9d option when you right-click a binary. The next step is to run \xe2\x80\x9csdclt.exe /Kickoffelev\xe2\x80\x9d with procmon running. After going through the output, we see the trusty \xe2\x80\x9cshell\\<verb>\\command\xe2\x80\x9d registry search path in the HKEY_CURRENT_USER hive. The next step was to add those keys and see if our binary and parameters of choice would execute. Unfortunately, nothing executed after adding the keys and starting \xe2\x80\x9csdclt.exe /kickoffelev\xe2\x80\x9d. Looking back in procmon, our keys are queried, but sdclt.exe is actually looking for an additional value within the \xe2\x80\x9ccommand\xe2\x80\x9d key: \xe2\x80\x9cIsolatedCommand\xe2\x80\x9d. We can then add our payload and parameters in a string (REG_SZ) value within the \xe2\x80\x9cCommand\xe2\x80\x9d key called \xe2\x80\x9cIsolatedCommand\xe2\x80\x9d: This is the same bug (minus the IsolatedCommand portion) that was used in the eventvwr.exe \xe2\x80\x9cfileless\xe2\x80\x9d UAC bypass. You can read about the eventvwr.exe bypass and the specific registry keys used here. Notice that instead of \xe2\x80\x9cshell\\open\\command\xe2\x80\x9d, we now see \xe2\x80\x9cshell\\runas\\command\xe2\x80\x9d. This is because sdclt.exe was invoked (again) using the \xe2\x80\x9cRunAs\xe2\x80\x9d verb via SxShellExecuteWithElevate. After adding our payload as the \xe2\x80\x9cIsolatedCommand\xe2\x80\x9d value, running \xe2\x80\x9csdclt.exe /KickOffElev\xe2\x80\x9d will execute our payload (and any parameters) in a high-integrity context: To demonstrate this technique, you can find a script here:\xc2 https://github.com/enigma0x3/Misc-PowerShell-Stuff/blob/master/Invoke-SDCLTBypass.ps1 The script takes a full path to your payload and any parameters. \xe2\x80\x9cC:\\Windows\\System32\\cmd.exe /c notepad.exe\xe2\x80\x9d is a good one to validate. It will automatically add the keys, start \xe2\x80\x9csdclt.exe /kickoffelev\xe2\x80\x9d and then cleanup. This particular technique can be remediated or fixed by setting the UAC level to \xe2\x80\x9cAlways Notify\xe2\x80\x9d or by removing the current user from the Local Administrators group. Further, if you would like to monitor for this attack, you could utilize methods/signatures to look for and alert on new registry entries in HKCU:\\Software\\Classes\\exefile\\shell\\runas\\command\\isolatedCommand Cheers, Matt Share this: Twitter Facebook Like this: Like Loading...
